A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AEM research, with readable text, equations, tables and figures. The supplied v1 ends with references; v2 adds Appendices A–E. All supplied material supports comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original mistake-detection experiments on EgoPER and CaptainCook4D, component ablations, action-segmentation results and qualitative examples.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds VLM, segmentation and prompt comparisons, plus an original manual evaluation of scene recognition.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1–3.6 retain the same AEM architecture, sampling procedure, objectives and prompt-based detector. Appendix A supplies previously missing implementation details, including failed-extraction masking, without establishing that the underlying algorithm was revised.

E1.justification: The cooking datasets and procedural tasks remain EgoPER and CaptainCook4D. Appendix B.4 adds a separately evaluated auxiliary task: judging recognized object attributes and spatial relations against human assessments on EgoPER frames.

E2.justification: The external baselines in Tables 1–3 remain unchanged. Appendix B extends the scene-generator comparison with GPT-5 and adds fixed textual prompts as a comparator to the proposed learnable prompts.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark splits and metrics remain unchanged. Added diagnostic settings include ground-truth segmentation only during inference and fixed-prompt/GPT-5 variants. The new recognition audit specifies 100 scenes, 20 per recipe, divided between two annotators, with scene-success and item-accuracy metrics.

E4.justification: Appendix B substantially expands diagnostic evidence by testing segmentation dependence, learnable-prompt benefits, GPT-5 supervision and scene-recognition reliability. Appendix C adds graph and frame-selection examples and qualitative findings about using multiple effect frames. These address important component dependencies beyond v1’s retained ablations.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, confidence intervals, error bars or significance tests. The new audit reports point estimates. Appendix D discusses stochastic model outputs and proposes fixed seeds as future mitigation, without introducing a replication or uncertainty-estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain their values. New results include GPT-5 AUC/EDA of 74.0/67.5, ground-truth-segmentation results of 86.7/74.7, fixed-prompt results of 72.8/63.5, and reported recognition success/accuracy of 48.4%/87.0%. These substantially extend the evidence under additional conditions; they are not improvements to unchanged experimental settings.

T1.justification: The probabilistic factorization, conditional-independence assumption, representation definitions and objectives in Equations 1–10 remain unchanged. The appendix adds implementation pseudocode and ordinary evaluation definitions, without new theoretical results, proofs or derivations.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same contributions: probabilistic action-effect modeling, complementary state/relation supervision and a prompt-based detector. The central benchmark-performance and execution-plus-outcome claims remain unchanged; the conclusion mainly expands future directions.

C2.justification: Appendices B–D add substantive interpretations of segmentation bottlenecks, prompt interference and multi-frame noise/cost. Limitations expand to occlusion, unreliable detection, stochastic supervision, domain/resource constraints and limited mistake interpretability. These considerably deepen v1’s narrower discussion of noise and future multi-step reasoning.

D1.justification: Appendix A supplies dynamic-fusion operations, complete GPT prompts, graph-processing pseudocode, a worked example and failed-extraction handling. This fills substantial documentation gaps behind v1’s unresolved appendix reference. v2 also adds a project-page reference, although the PDFs alone do not establish code availability.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to Li and Liang’s prefix-tuning work and GPT-5, supporting the appended experiments and methodological attribution. The related-work coverage and positioning against execution-focused mistake detection remain essentially unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative remains largely verbatim, with localized wording edits, a shortened affiliation and repaired appendix references. v2 organizes supplementary material into Appendices A–E and adds acknowledgments and an LLM-use disclosure, without extensively rewriting the retained sections.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figures 5–10, Tables 4–6 and two algorithm blocks, including architecture diagrams, prompts, an annotation interface and frame-score visualizations. Figure 4 is enlarged and rearranged while retaining its examples. These substantially expand the paper’s visual and tabular presentation.

improvement.justification: v2 improves assessability through implementation details, targeted component tests, a supervision audit and explicit limitations. These gains are tempered by new inconsistencies: Algorithm 2 omits relation-to-object edges depicted in Figure 6, and the reported 48.4% scene-success rate is unexplained under the stated 100-scene, equally divided audit. The additions provide a positive but qualified improvement; the main benchmark evidence remains unchanged.
